Latest Update: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1386 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide new directions for muscular dystrophy treatments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue. But scientists have discovered that without one critical protein, this repair system can break down, leaving injured muscles filled with fat and scar tissue instead of healthy muscle.

It has been revealed that researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes. Their findings suggest that TRF2 is also essential for maintaining the identity of muscle stem cells, allowing them to continue repairing and regenerating muscle throughout life.

It has been revealed that the discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide new directions for muscular dystrophy treatments. It may also help scientists understand important differences between muscle regeneration and cancer, including why skeletal muscle can repair itself so effectively while cancers originating in muscle are relatively uncommon.

"For years, TRF2 has been viewed as a protein whose primary job is protecting the ends of chromosomes from damage or corruption," said senior author Foteini Mourkioti, PhD, an associate professor of Orthopedic Surgery at Penn Medicine. "But rather than simply protecting DNA, TRF2 seems to be key to regenerating muscle throughout life.".

A Hidden Protein With an Unexpected Role in Muscle Repair.

In a recent development, for years, scientists have studied TRF2 because of its role in safeguarding telomeres, the protective structures found at the ends of chromosomes. Chromosomes carry our genetic information, and telomeres help keep their ends from deteriorating or being mistaken for damaged DNA.

The latest research indicates that TRF2 has another notable responsibility. It helps muscle stem cells retain the genetic instructions that make them muscle stem cells in the first place. Maintaining that identity is essential because these specialized cells serve as the body's reserve supply for repairing injured muscle.

Recent findings suggest that under normal conditions, muscle stem cells spend much of their time inactive. When an injury occurs, they become active, multiply, and help replace damaged muscle tissue. Some then return to a resting state, preserving a population of stem cells that can respond to future injuries.

It has been revealed that through laboratory experiments, the researchers found that TRF2 levels change as muscle stem cells move between these different stages. The protein's activity rises and falls as the cells transition from dormancy to repair and then replenish themselves, suggesting that TRF2 helps regulate the entire regeneration process.

Without TRF2, Damaged Muscles Accumulate Fat and Scar Tissue.

Recent findings suggest that to understand how important TRF2 is, the scientists removed the protein from muscle stem cells in laboratory mice. At first, the animals' muscles appeared normal, suggesting that the loss of TRF2 did not immediately damage existing muscle tissue.

Sources indicate that over time, however, a serious problem emerged. The population of functional muscle stem cells began to decline, leaving the animals increasingly unable to repair damaged muscle.

The researchers initially expected the cells to die, since losing TRF2 can produce that outcome in other tissues. Instead, they discovered something more surprising: the cells remained alive but lost the molecular identity that allowed them to function as muscle stem cells.

In effect, the cells no longer maintained the biological program needed to perform their specialized repair duties.

Recent findings suggest that the consequences became clear when the muscles were injured. Rather than rebuilding healthy muscle, the damaged tissue accumulated fat and scar tissue, a form of tissue replacement that cannot restore normal muscle function.

"This completely changes how we think about TRF2's role in these cells," mentioned Mourkioti. "The loss of identity has severe implications for whether recovery from injury is even possible.".

A Potential Breakthrough for Muscular Dystrophy Research.

The team also investigated whether TRF2 plays a role in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a serious inherited disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The disease interferes with the body's ability to maintain healthy muscles, making effective repair especially important.

Using a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the researchers removed TRF2 from muscle stem cells and observed a dramatic worsening of the disease.

Muscle degeneration progressed much faster, and the affected mice had shorter survival times. These findings indicate that TRF2 plays an notable role in preserving the regenerative capacity of muscles already struggling with a serious genetic disease.

In a recent development, the results do not yet establish a new treatment for muscular dystrophy. However, they identify a biological mechanism that researchers may eventually be able to target to help preserve muscle stem cell function and improve tissue repair.

How TRF2 Protects the Identity of Muscle Stem Cells.

Further experiments revealed how TRF2 performs this unexpected function.

Although the protein is best known for working at the ends of chromosomes, the researchers found that it also attaches to regulatory regions throughout the genome. These regions help control which genes are active or inactive, determining how cells behave and what specialized functions they perform.

It has been revealed that for muscle stem cells, this regulation is particularly crucial. Their ability to repair muscle depends on maintaining a specific pattern of gene activity that preserves their identity and regenerative potential.

The scientists discovered that many of the DNA regions associated with TRF2 contain unusual structures known as G-quadruplexes. These structures form when sections of DNA rich in the building block guanine fold into distinctive arrangements involving four interacting strands or segments.

Industry observers note that G-quadruplexes have attracted considerable scientific interest because they can influence how genes function. They are also being investigated as possible targets for cancer treatments.

The Penn researchers found that TRF2 interacts with these specialized DNA structures to help maintain the genetic program that keeps muscle stem cells functioning properly.

"We found that TRF2 works through these secondary DNA structures to preserve the identity of muscle stem cells and keep them capable of repairing damaged muscle," Mourkioti stated. "That was completely unexpected.".

What Muscle Regeneration Could Reveal About Cancer.

Beyond muscular dystrophy, the discovery may help researchers investigate a longstanding mystery about muscle biology.

Skeletal muscle, the type of muscle that allows the body to move, has an impressive ability to regenerate after injury. Yet cancers that originate in skeletal muscle are relatively rare, even though other tissues with substantial regenerative activity can be more vulnerable to cancer.

This raises an vital question: how can muscle maintain such a powerful repair system without frequently developing cancer?

The researchers believe that TRF2's unusual role in muscle stem cells could offer clues. By examining how the protein regulates gene activity in muscle compared with other tissues, scientists may gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that support regeneration while limiting the risk of uncontrolled cell growth.

That distinction matters because cancer develops when cells acquire changes that allow them to grow and divide without the normal biological restraints. Finding ways to strengthen muscle repair without encouraging abnormal growth would be an important goal for future therapies.

It has been revealed that mourkioti and her colleagues are now investigating whether the way muscle stem cells use TRF2 could lead to fresh treatment strategies for muscular dystrophy. They also hope to determine what this mechanism can reveal about cancer biology in tissues that are more susceptible to the disease.

It has been revealed that although additional research is needed to determine whether these findings can be translated into treatments for people, the discovery reveals an important part of the body's muscle repair system. It also demonstrates that a protein long associated with protecting DNA has a much broader role in keeping muscles capable of healing.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health/ National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (R01 DK123356, R01s CA174904, GM101149, and FDN-143330).

It has been revealed that materials provided by University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations.
  • That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA initiative Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth said in its complaint that it is bring the lawsuit to "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

Industry observers note that the star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare proposal finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A initiative’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

According to recent reports, UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The tech giant sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the manufacturer said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the organization noted.

According to recent reports, in addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company noted.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the looks available to them," Elevance stated.

Industry observers note that "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans.".

UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

Industry observers note that the court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The tech giant remarked that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the firm's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

In a recent development, "The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in prepares with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the tech giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene indicates that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

Sources indicate that the use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the manufacturer, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in intends with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the firm said in the lawsuit.

In a recent development, CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the tech giant estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 initiative year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the organization and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company stated in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, prepares, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to blueprint payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment stated in the lawsuit.

According to recent reports, the company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about initiative enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company remarked. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in aims with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the organization tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment stated in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.

Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S.
  • The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS).
  • It has been revealed that both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). Women with greater concentrations of these substances in their blood were more likely to develop this type of cancer. However, researchers found no clear link between either chemical and breast cancer risk overall.

It has been revealed that both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS. These chemicals have been used in numerous everyday consumer products and are often described as "forever chemicals" because they resist breaking down in the environment. They can also accumulate in the human body and remain there for years.

"Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health," stated HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. "This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump's leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.".

Why This Aggressive Breast Cancer Is Concerning.

Sources indicate that ER-negative breast cancer differs from more common forms of the disease because its tumor cells lack the receptors that allow estrogen to stimulate cancer growth. These cancers are often more aggressive and generally have poorer outcomes than tumors that respond to estrogen.

Despite their severity, researchers still have relatively little information about what makes someone more likely to develop ER-negative breast cancer. The new findings suggest that exposure to certain persistent environmental chemicals could be one contributing factor.

"Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors," explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study.

The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

Higher Forever Chemical Levels Linked to Greater Cancer Risk.

To investigate the possible connection, NIH scientists and their collaborators examined blood samples that had been collected years before participants received a cancer diagnosis. The researchers measured concentrations of 17 different PFAS chemicals, allowing them to compare earlier exposure levels with subsequent breast cancer outcomes.

Industry observers note that the results revealed substantial differences for two chemicals. Women in the highest PFOA exposure group had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than women in the lowest group. The association was even stronger for PFOS, with the highest exposure group showing a 93% higher rate, nearly twice that of the lowest group.

These percentages represent relative differences between groups rather than the absolute probability that an individual woman will develop breast cancer. The findings also establish an association, not proof that the chemicals directly cause the disease.

Recent findings suggest that the analysis used data from the Sister Study, a major research project conducted by NIH's National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). Between 2003 and 2009, the study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35-74 from across the United States and Puerto Rico.

Recent findings suggest that all participants were free of breast cancer when they enrolled, although each had a full or half-sister who had already been diagnosed with the disease. For the PFAS investigation, researchers analyzed information from 1,609 women who subsequently developed breast cancer and a comparison group of 2,269 women.

Could Reducing PFAS Exposure Lower Cancer Risk?

Although PFAS can remain in the environment and the body for long periods, researchers emphasize that exposure is not necessarily unavoidable. The findings could eventually help identify upcoming ways to reduce the risk of aggressive breast cancer.

It has been revealed that "These findings matter for women's health broadly," noted first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., who previously worked as an NIH research fellow and is now a researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. "Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention.".

In a recent development, the researchers are also interested in understanding how these chemicals might influence cancer development. Because the strongest associations appeared in tumors that lack estrogen receptors, the findings suggest that PFAS could act through biological processes unrelated to hormonal signaling.

It has been revealed that potential explanations include changes in gene activity or alterations in the immune system. However, the study did not directly investigate these mechanisms, so their involvement remains uncertain.

Newer Forever Chemicals Raise Unanswered Questions.

Although PFOA and PFOS have largely been phased out and replaced with other PFAS compounds, measurable amounts of both substances are still present in most people's bodies. Their persistence means that exposure to these older chemicals remains a potential public health concern.

It has been revealed that the researchers say additional investigations should focus on populations with greater PFAS exposure, as well as groups that experience higher rates of ER-negative breast cancer. Such research could help clarify the strength of the observed associations and identify whether certain populations face greater risks.

Scientists also need to determine whether the newer chemicals introduced as replacements for PFOA and PFOS carry similar health concerns.

"More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals," White said.

The findings add to growing questions about the long-term health effects of forever chemicals and highlight the importance of understanding how environmental exposures may contribute to aggressive forms of breast cancer.

The research received support from NIEHS grants Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.

Industry News: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major upcoming study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks.
  • The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago.
  • An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major upcoming study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks. However, the findings also point to a possible increase in risk over a longer period, making the decision more complicated than it initially appears.

The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago. The annual conference brings together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, emerging evidence, and advances in clinical care.

An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes. Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol and reduce these risks, including in people who have never experienced a cardiovascular event. This preventive approach remains a central part of the American Heart Association's 2026 joint guideline on dyslipidemia.

Do Older Adults Need to Keep Taking Statins?

Although statins are an established treatment for reducing cardiovascular risk, questions remain about how much benefit they provide when people reach their 70s and beyond, particularly if they have never had a heart attack or stroke.

It has been revealed that "While the Association's recent joint guideline recommends lifestyle and potentially medication for people with high LDL-C at younger ages to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, recent studies question the health benefits of continuing statins in the later decades of life," stated study author Rita F. Redberg, M.D., M.Sc., FAHA, professor of cardiology and the Araxe Vilensky Endowed Chair in Cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. "A few previous studies assessed the safety of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at age 70 and later, and they found no difference in mortality. One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins. Whether it is safe to discontinue statins to prevent a first CVD event in the elderly remained unclear and the question we explored in our study.".

To investigate, researchers enrolled nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who were taking statins specifically to prevent a first cardiovascular event. Every participant also had at least two chronic medical conditions, such as a history of cancer or lung disease.

Recent findings suggest that participants were divided into two groups. One group stopped taking statins, while the other continued their prescribed treatment. Researchers tracked their health for approximately two years, with additional follow-up extending as long as four years. They examined rates of heart attack, stroke, and death, along with changes in quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and muscle wasting (known as sarcopenia).

What Happened When Older Adults Stopped Statins?

It has been revealed that the initial findings were largely reassuring. After approximately two years, participants who stopped taking statins did not experience a statistically significant increase in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths compared with those who remained on the medications.

It has been revealed that stopping treatment also did not produce measurable improvements in the other outcomes researchers examined. Quality of life, muscle discomfort, falls, and muscle wasting were similar in both groups.

In a recent development, there was, however, a small difference in cardiovascular outcomes. Over the first two years, the results indicated approximately one additional cardiovascular event for every 40 people who discontinued statins compared with those who continued treatment.

It has been revealed that the longer follow-up revealed a more concerning pattern. Over a period of up to four years, 12.7% of participants who stopped statins experienced a heart attack, stroke, or death, compared with 9.2% of those who kept taking the medications.

Longer Follow-Up Reveals a Potential Risk.

Redberg explained that the higher rate of serious outcomes during the four-year follow-up represents a latest finding in research on statin discontinuation among older adults. She suggested that the difference may have emerged because this trial included more participants and tracked them for a longer period than earlier studies.

These results complicate the question of whether older adults should continue cholesterol treatment indefinitely. While the findings suggest that stopping statins may be a reasonable option for many people in this age group, they also indicate that remaining on treatment could offer some protection over time.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," she remarked. "There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event.".

Study Design and Notable Limitations.

According to recent reports, the trial involved 1,880 participants aged 70 and older (average age of 77; 53% men, and 47% women), all of whom had at least two chronic health conditions. Individuals with established cardiovascular disease or a previous cardiovascular event were not eligible to participate.

Researchers conducted the study between November 2021 and April 2026 across 24 medical centers in Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. Of the participants, 938 were assigned to discontinue statins, while 942 were assigned to continue taking their medications.

According to recent reports, throughout the trial and subsequent follow-up, researchers recorded heart attacks, acute ischemic strokes, and deaths from any cause. Participants also completed surveys assessing their overall quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and sarcopenia.

Industry observers note that one limitation was that some participants did not remain in their originally assigned groups. Some people instructed to stop statins eventually resumed treatment, while others assigned to continue taking statins stopped using them. Altogether, approximately 14% of participants switched from their assigned treatment approach during the study.

According to recent reports, to determine whether these changes affected the findings, the researchers performed several additional statistical analyses. The results remained unchanged.

Taken together, the findings suggest that discontinuing statins may be an option for many adults over 70 who have not previously experienced cardiovascular disease, especially when considering outcomes over the first two years. However, the higher rate of heart attacks, strokes, and deaths during longer follow-up underscores why stopping treatment should be an individualized decision made with a healthcare professional rather than a general recommendation for all older adults.

#19024. Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put.
  • The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.
  • Industry observers note that the Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put. But helping free up housing in these districts isn't as simple as getting older people to move, a new study argues.

The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.

Industry observers note that the Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts. But it pinned that on affordability challenges. Higher-income households of all types compete for housing in the best-performing school districts.

This is a conundrum for neighborhoods. Seniors are thus left in neighborhoods paying premiums for school districts they don't use. Meanwhile young families who'd like move into the district face limited options for homes there.

Sources indicate that of course, many seniors want to age in place in homes that they've lived in for decades. But others looking to downsize are "locked in" due to high mortgage rates. That can leave them in homes that they can't afford or, worse, in homes that pose safety risks for aging people.

"These findings suggest that policies aimed solely at encouraging older households to downsize are unlikely to substantially improve access to quality school districts," the paper says.

Low housing turnover in these districts drives up prices. The higher-rated public school districts are, on average, 49% more expensive, and homes there move faster, Realtor.com® data indicates. But in some of the nation's top school districts—including in Dallas, Los Angeles, and San Fransisco—homes can sell for three times the price of surrounding metros.

Using data from the American Community Survey, the Cleveland Fed found that households over 65 occupy a disproportionate share of the housing stock in the best-performing school districts. While these account for 26.2% of all households nationally, they make up as much as 28.7% of households in the least affordable areas.

Meanwhile households with children, which make up about 31.2% of U.S. households, occupy 30.1% of housing in the best school districts and 40% of the housing stock in the lowest-quality districts. The same doesn't ring true for one-person households, which tend to be more evenly distributed.

Older homeowners move at about the same rate across all school districts—about 6.9% a year. About 81% of older adults in the best school districts own their homes. To the Cleveland Fed, that shows older households aren't limiting turnover of housing stock in high-quality and high-cost districts.

Recent findings suggest that "While older households occupy a modestly larger share of housing in these expensive, high-quality areas, they do not appear to limit turnover," the paper states. "These patterns suggest that the challenge of accessing high-quality school districts is driven by a combination of income sorting and competition from multiple household types rather than solely by empty-nesters’ aging in place.".

In a recent development, realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu says a few complications are affecting seniors as they consider their futures. They include capital gains taxes they'd incur on homes that have appreciated in value. They also include the kinds of taxes they'd incur when they move to a new place. Then there are the social considerations.

"Right-sized, single-level, accessible homes near family and doctors are scarce," Xu claims. "Moving also means leaving behind the neighbors and community that owners have built over decades. For many longtime owners, there are few good places to go.".

In a recent development, buyers can still find deals in some of these good markets, Realtor.com found, if they look carefully. But in some good districts, there simply aren't a lot of homes changing hands.

According to recent reports, xu adds that she's surprised that young professionals without children can also compete for housing in these expensive districts. Jobs, urban amenities, and investment opportunity for the real estate tend to make these areas attractive.

In a recent development, "Even if more seniors moved, the homes they left would likely go to higher-income buyers, because this is a sorting story. The districts wouldn’t become much more affordable," Xu claims. "The more direct solution is building more homes in and near high-demand districts. Adding right-sized options could also give older owners who want to move somewhere to go, but supply is what would ease pressure on prices.".

To Arick Morton, CEO of NIC MAP, the frozen market points to a need for more housing oriented toward seniors. Earlier this year, his group stated the nation needs to add 1 million new senior housing units by 2040. That $1 trillion homebuilding frenzy would meet the moment 10 million baby boomers pass age 80.

"People stay at home much longer than they did previously," Morton mentioned. "Of course folks stay at home as long as they can and then movie into senior housing when the need is there.".

But when there isn't enough senior housing or they don't have good alternatives to downsize, those seniors end up displaced when age or an accident means they require more intensive care needs.

"The best policy options are those that help expedite the construction of senior housing," Morton mentioned. "We don't have enough capacity to create a dent in that logjam.".

Sources indicate that tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

Sources indicate that chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co. Ltd. today announced it has raised $200 million in upcoming funding to invest in its core technology and expand its automated life sciences infrastructure for increasingly complex physical systems.

Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.

Investors joining the round included Oman Investment Authority, Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia, Sinovation Ventures and CMB International. The firm raised $600 million to date across multiple funding rounds, including nearly $300 million in Series C during 2022.

Sources indicate that “The first generation of AI learned from humanity’s accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world — through experiments, production and continuous feedback,” said founder and Chief Executive Daniel Huang. “That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create newly introduced knowledge, materials, processes and products.”.

According to recent reports, the company’s two most prominently marketed offerings are Megalaxy Lab, an AI-connected experimental platform and CellVue T2000, its automated cell-imaging instrument. Both appear on the company’s English-language homepage. MegaRobo also sells more specialized lab equipment, including the Auflo sample-preparation workstation and the Seloris cell culturing automation system.

The key distinction is that Megalaxy Lab is the public face for the company’s AI-for-science strategy, while CellVue and other systems represent concrete examples of the instruments it builds for the industry.

Industry observers note that the company stated through Megalaxy it is making real-world experimentation programmable and accessible. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them through automated laboratory systems, track execution, receive structured, machine-readable results, and feed them directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. This includes virtual large data readouts that can be amplified as digital twins representing the scientific data, protein design, biochemistry and other properties.

MegaRobo remarked it’s working together with industry partners, including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, to expand its capability in the AI Science community with the launch of Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity to test models against real experimental data.

Sources indicate that the tech giant is also developing the One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for instruments, machines, materials processes and real-world feedback. It’s not just a collection of isolated AI applications and products, but a chain infrastructure that enables AI to act, learn and observe across complex physical environments.

#19022. Latest Update: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (993 w)

Latest Update: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smile might brighten your mood, but latest research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect.
  • Recent findings suggest that for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier.
  • According to recent reports, "I used to work in customer service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smile might brighten your mood, but latest research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

Recent findings suggest that for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

According to recent reports, "I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world.".

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an notable distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness.

Industry observers note that to explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

"We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles said. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile.".

In a recent development, the online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others revealed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

Industry observers note that during the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

Sources indicate that to introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

When Fake Smiles Start to Backfire.

After completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results revealed that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

When participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

The pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

Further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

"If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he said. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse.".

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work.

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

Industry observers note that the issue has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

The problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

After spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we currently are," he mentioned, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have.".

Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but newly introduced research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference.
  • Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected.
  • Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but newly introduced research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference. A clinical trial led by researchers at La Trobe University found that supervised exercise and education can improve knee health, reduce pain, and enhance quality of life in young adults recovering from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The findings also offer hope for addressing their elevated risk of developing knee osteoarthritis at an unusually young age.

Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected. About half of patients are still dissatisfied with their knee health two years after the procedure. Even more concerning, roughly half develop signs of early-onset knee osteoarthritis within a decade, often before reaching age 40.

Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations. One obstacle is the widespread concern, shared by some patients and healthcare professionals, that exercise could damage already vulnerable knee cartilage.

A New Approach to Recovery After ACL Surgery.

Sources indicate that to investigate whether additional rehabilitation could help, researchers at La Trobe University's Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre conducted the SUPER-Knee clinical trial. It was the first study to evaluate the benefits of combining exercise therapy and education more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a time when patients are generally expected to have recovered even though many continue to experience problems.

According to recent reports, the researchers enrolled 184 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 who were still struggling with knee symptoms one to three years after their operations. Participants were assigned to either a progressive exercise therapy program or a comparison group that received a single educational session.

The findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, highlighted that participants who completed the four-month program under the guidance of a physical therapist experienced improvements in knee health and muscle strength, along with less pain and better quality of life.

Importantly, these benefits came without evidence that the exercises were damaging knee cartilage or worsening early osteoarthritis. The results challenge the belief that physical activity necessarily makes injured knees worse.

Exercise Offers Hope Against Early Knee Osteoarthritis.

Associate Professor Adam Culvenor, who led the research, said the findings provide much-needed evidence about how to help younger patients who remain at risk of knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery.

"Right now we don't have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority," Associate Professor Culvenor said.

"Our study highlighted physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.

"The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to update international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.

"The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training.".

Industry observers note that the findings could influence how clinicians approach rehabilitation long after ACL surgery, particularly for patients whose symptoms continue beyond the usual recovery period. Although the trial did not establish whether the program prevents osteoarthritis over the long term, it demonstrated that supervised exercise can improve knee health without accelerating the cartilage damage or early osteoarthritis researchers were monitoring.

Years of Knee Pain After a Serious Sports Injury.

Recent findings suggest that for Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovering from ACL surgery were deeply personal. In 2019, when she was 24, she tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football. Hoping to return to the sport as quickly as possible, she underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks.

In a recent development, but the operation did not lead to the recovery she had imagined. Her rehabilitation continued for years, and she ultimately decided not to return to football.

"I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I'd be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life - not just footy - I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven't played contact sport since," Ruby said.

"Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me.".

According to recent reports, cumming remained committed to her rehabilitation, regularly attending physical therapy appointments and performing prescribed exercises. She initially exercised daily before moving to a weekly routine. Despite those efforts, she continued to experience varying degrees of knee pain every day for three to four years.

Her experience changed after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee trial and began participating in weekly rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physical therapist.

"When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly," Ruby stated.

In a recent development, the research suggests that people who continue to struggle after ACL reconstruction may benefit from additional structured rehabilitation, even years after their original injury. Because the program requires little specialized equipment or additional staff training, researchers say healthcare professionals could readily incorporate it into existing treatment services.

The SUPER-Knee clinical trial received funding through a Project Grant from Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

#19018. A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (881 w)

A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates.
  • Industry observers note that one possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

Industry observers note that one possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A newly introduced study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies.

To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

Industry observers note that solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly key.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

In a recent development, another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals Upcoming Clues to Math Difficulties.

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

In a recent development, the findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

According to recent reports, such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change aims when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

Sources indicate that the Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide fresh evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children.

In a recent development, an important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes.".

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

Industry observers note that the findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises pushing AI from pilot to production are learning that data, not GPUs, is the hardest part, and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg are part of the answer.
  • In a recent development, that pressure is turning storage into an active layer that classifies, governs and serves data to models.
  • It has been revealed that “Storage is not seen as just storing the data,” Raman said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:39 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Enterprises pushing AI from pilot to production are learning that data, not GPUs, is the hardest part, and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg are part of the answer. Demand for AI infrastructure shows few signs of slowing, but much of the information companies need is still scattered, ungoverned and out of reach.

In a recent development, that pressure is turning storage into an active layer that classifies, governs and serves data to models. Unstructured files such as logs and medical images hold intelligence AI can now extract, according to Arun Prasad Raman (pictured, left), vice president of hybrid cloud and AI infrastructure at Hitachi Vantara Corp.

It has been revealed that “Storage is not seen as just storing the data,” Raman said. “You need to bring in more intelligence natively rather than moving the data to another replication and bringing it back for, say, indexing. If it can do it natively, that’s where the value add is.”.

Industry observers note that raman and Jeff Lundberg (right), principal product and solutions manager at Hitachi Vantara, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI’s pilot-to-production gap, Apache Iceberg and how Hitachi Vantara is adding intelligence to storage. (* Disclosure below.).

Reference architectures for AI factories and data platforms are largely settled. Most projects stall because data is spread across on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications and the cloud, while access control, governance and shifting regulations add friction, according to Lundberg. Hitachi Vantara is responding with industry-specific solutions built on its Hitachi iQ stack and its sister businesses’ rail and energy experience, he explained.

“It’s about the outcome more so than the technology that we’re trying to put into place,” Lundberg remarked. “That’s an enabler to get you to the solution you’re trying to get to.”.

Recent findings suggest that much of that work now happens in storage. Last week, Hitachi Vantara expanded its VSP One platform with new object storage and data lakehouse capabilities. A service in its object store flags files containing personal information, such as Social Security numbers. Data scientists can then keep that data out of specific models or block its replication to another country, Raman explained.

Industry observers note that “That’s the intelligence we are adding into the storage itself,” Raman said. “So that’s where the evolution of storage is making it more intelligent.”.

Analytics follow the same logic. CT scan metadata can be stored in Apache Iceberg format on the organization’s object store and queried directly. An application could list every abdominal scan from the past year without a separate extract, transform and load or ETL process or database, Raman noted.

In a recent development, “Whether it’s a backup or it’s 10 years old, it still carries some intelligence,” Raman noted. “As long as it carries intelligence, it becomes notable to AI.”.

A newly introduced fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising newly introduced way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
  • The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.
  • Recent findings suggest that IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising newly introduced way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have developed and tested a fiber combination that supports beneficial gut bacteria without making common digestive symptoms worse.

The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

Recent findings suggest that IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians. Although its exact cause remains unclear, stress, infections, and certain medications may contribute to the condition. Symptoms can also become worse because of particular foods, inadequate sleep, psychological stress, hormonal changes, and lifestyle factors.

Why Common IBS Diets Can Affect Gut Health.

People with IBS are frequently advised to follow a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that are easily fermented by gut bacteria. Although this approach can help control uncomfortable symptoms, restricting these foods may also have unintended consequences for the gut microbiome.

Industry observers note that "For years we've known that a diet low in Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monesaccharides and Polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time," lead author Dr. Tina Yan said.

"We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet.".

The new findings suggest that a carefully formulated fiber supplement could help address this problem, allowing people with IBS to support a healthier gut microbiome while continuing to manage their symptoms through dietary changes.

The researchers attribute the supplement's promising effects to its combination of two ingredients: resistant starch and psyllium husk.

Recent findings suggest that psyllium appears to slow the breakdown of resistant starch by gut bacteria, allowing more of it to reach deeper sections of the colon before fermentation occurs. This process may increase the production of beneficial compounds that support intestinal health.

In a recent development, ordinarily, fermentable fiber can be challenging for people with IBS because bacterial fermentation can produce excess gas and increase digestive discomfort. The fresh formulation appears to offer a way to obtain the benefits of fermentation without aggravating these symptoms.

"Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort," Dr. Yan said.

"What's exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety.".

Significant Changes in Gut Bacteria and Anxiety.

The researchers observed substantial shifts in the composition of participants' gut bacteria during the intervention. These changes were particularly notable because they occurred over a relatively short period.

"Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention," ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine mentioned.

Sources indicate that "The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see.".

Alongside improvements in gut bacteria, participants also experienced reductions in gut-related anxiety. These findings suggest that the supplement's potential benefits may extend beyond changes in the digestive system, although further research will be needed to establish its broader effects.

A Latest Approach to Managing Irritable Bowel Syndrome.

The researchers believe their findings could help shift IBS care toward improving the underlying health of the gut rather than focusing exclusively on avoiding foods that cause discomfort.

"For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods," ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen remarked.

In a recent development, "Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That's an important step forward.".

By demonstrating that beneficial gut bacteria can be supported without increasing IBS symptoms, the study points toward fresh dietary strategies that could complement existing treatments.

Industry observers note that the ur gut® supplement is already available for purchase. The research team has also created a cookbook featuring recipes designed to help people incorporate the supplement into a healthy diet.

The study, "Dietary fibre blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomised, double-blind control trial," was published online in the European Journal of Nutrition.
